results.title: Detecting Moderator Effects Using Subgroup Analyses
results.content: In the analysis of prevention and intervention studies, it is often important to investigate whether treatment effects vary among subgroups of patients defined by individual characteristics. Multiple authors have argued that, to assess whether a treatment effect varies across subgroups defined by patient characteristics, analyses should be based on tests for interaction rather than treatment comparisons within the subgroups. Subgroup difference tests were performed to determine whether the effect of the 5-HTTLPR interaction varies significantly among subgroups of studies defined by temporal factors as duration of stress and time interval between end of stress and assessment of depression [34]. Properly conducted and reported moderator analyses allow researchers to assess whether a treatment effect varies across subgroups defined by participant characteristics, and clinicians to target interventions to specific patient subpopulations. 1 If differences between the groups are statistically or clinically relevant in a prespecified analysis, we may declare the characteristic defining them an important effect measure modifier (EMM) (sometimes referred to as "effect moderation," "statistical interaction," or "heterogeneity of effect") [2][3][4][5] and rely on each subgroup's estimate to understand the potential magnitude(s) of the treatment effect. Another limitation is that despite the moderate size of the overall sample, for certain interaction variables, the number of students in some subgroups was very small (<10), which may lead to less power for detecting statistical significance of interaction effects of control variables and subgroup differences (Wang & Ware, 2013). Theories and results should be tested for robustness in subgroups analysis to elaborate specific prevention and intervention options based on moderator analysis (e.g., Wang & Ware, 2013), in terms, for example, of the growing population of nontraditional students in higher education (Wild et al., 2023b). In this case study, leveraging the biobank and electronic health record data in the Partner Health System, we introduce a new data analysis pipeline and a novel statistical methodology that address existing limitations by (i) designing a rigorous causal framework that systematically examines the causal effects of statin usage on T2D risk in observational data, (ii) uncovering which patient subgroup is most vulnerable for developing T2D after taking statins, and (iii) assessing the replicability and statistical significance of the most vulnerable subgroup via a bootstrap calibration procedure.

Bayesian Hierarchical Models for Subgroup Analysis. In conventional subgroup analyses, subgroup treatment effects are estimated using data from each subgroup separately without considering data from other subgroups in the same study. A Bayesian hierarchical model (BHM) can be used to derive more precise, and less heterogenous estimates of subgroup treatment effects that are closer to the treatment effect in the overall population. In this article, we will discuss the technical details for applying one-way and multi-way BHM using summary-level statistics, and patient-level data for subgroup analysis. Four case studies based on four new drug applications are used to illustrate the application of these models in subgroup analyses for continuous, dichotomous, time-to-event, and count endpoints. **Keywords:** Bayesian hierarchical model; Drug Trial Snapshots; shrinkage analysis. * Subgroup analyses in randomised controlled trials: quantifying the risks of false-positives and false-negatives.Brookes ST, Whitley E, Peters TJ, Mulheran PA, Egger M, Davey Smith G.Brookes ST, et al.Health Technol Assess. * Investigating Stability in Subgroup Identification for Stratified Medicine.Hair GM, Jemielita T, Mt-Isa S, Schnell PM, Baumgartner R.Hair GM, et al.Pharm Stat. * The importance of "shrinkage" in subgroup analyses.Lipsky AM, Gausche-Hill M, Vienna M, Lewis RJ.Lipsky AM, et al.Ann Emerg Med. 2010 Jun;55(6):544-552.e3. * Bayesian cluster hierarchical model for subgroup borrowing in the design and analysis of basket trials with binary endpoints.Chen N, Lee JJ.Chen N, et al.Stat Methods Med Res. 2020 Sep;29(9):2717-2732. * A Bayesian approach to subgroup identification.Berger JO, Wang X, Shen L.Berger JO, et al.J Biopharm Stat. doi: 10.1080/10543406.2013.856026.J Biopharm Stat. “FDASIA Section 907: Inclusion of Demographic Subgroups in Clinical Trials,” accessed August 2, 2023,. “FDA Action Plan to Enhance the Collection and Availability of Demographic Subgroup Data,” accessed August 2, 2023,. results.title: Three simple rules to ensure reasonably credible subgroup analyses - PMC
results.content: * Categorical subgroup analyses should not be part of a typical clinical trial’s hypothesis testing analysis unless the prior probability for a subgroup effect being present is at least 20% and preferably higher than 50%. In both diagnostic testing and subgroup analyses, prior probability estimates are often unsettling given their inherent uncertainty and subjectivity, but failing to grapple with this tends to bias us towards falsely accepting new evidence as truth.10 Existing criteria to judge the credibility of subgroup analyses emphasise the importance of prior probability and specifically require that a hypothesis and its direction of effect are specified a priori and that the subgroup effect is supported by within-study empirical and biological evidence.6 In most cases, prior probability can be roughly estimated by thinking about the strength of previous theoretical or empirical evidence that the factor in question is likely to modify the relative treatment effect.11 Just as power for subgroups is usually much lower than for the main effect, so are the prior probabilities. \*Positive predictive values=probability that all reported positives analyses are true positives for a trial reporting at least one positive subgroup effect (that is, no false positives) for a given prior probability and power in the context of conducting one, five, or 10 subgroup comparisons without adjustment for multiple comparisons, assuming α=5% (0.05). Categorical subgroup analyses should not be part of a typical clinical trial’s primary (hypothesis testing) analysis unless the prior probability for a subgroup effect being present is at least 20% and preferably higher than 50%. Just as an excellent diagnostic test (sensitivity 99%, specificity 95%) results in a 20% positive predictive value if the prior probability of disease is 1%, only 20% of statistically significant subgroup effects will be true positives if the subgroup effect only had a 1% chance of occurring to begin with, even with 99% power. Careful consideration of the likelihood of a subgroup effect being present (prior probability) and the statistical power of the subgroup analysis (sensitivity) need to inform whether a subgroup analysis should be part of the primary (hypothesis testing) or exploratory (hypothesis generating) analyses.
